1. Overview: From MOS Capacitor to MOSFET

A roadmap connecting surface charge, capacitance, threshold voltage, and drain current.

A MOSFET is a MOS capacitor with two junctions added so that an inversion layer can carry current from source to drain. The core idea is therefore electrostatic: the gate voltage controls the surface potential, surface charge, channel charge, and finally the drain current.

MOS metaphor image: the gate bends the semiconductor surface, charge rearranges in response, and in a MOSFET the thin inversion puddle becomes a channel.
MOS Metaphor SimulatorStart with the embedded metaphor image, then open the full AI simulator for interactive gate-bias, C-V, and channel-flow exploration.
Electrostatics

Gate voltage divides between the oxide and semiconductor. Poisson's equation determines depletion charge and band bending.

Capacitance

The oxide capacitance and semiconductor depletion capacitance appear in series until strong inversion.

Transport

In a MOSFET, the inversion sheet conducts laterally. The channel can be resistive, pinched off, or weakly inverted.

Overview concept map from MOS capacitor to enhancement-type nMOS transistor and its I-V behavior. The sequence highlights how gate-controlled surface inversion in the MOS capacitor becomes a source-to-drain conduction channel in the transistor, which then produces cutoff, linear, and saturation operation in the output characteristics.
Reference sequence. The uploaded chapter begins with the ideal MOS capacitor, then develops accumulation, depletion, inversion, surface depletion, C-V behavior, nonideal oxide charge, and dielectric transport. This interactive chapter follows that sequence and extends it into MOSFET channel formation and I-V operation.

Core learning goals

  • Identify accumulation, depletion, weak inversion, and strong inversion from voltage, charge, and energy-band views.
  • Calculate oxide capacitance, depletion width, flat-band voltage, and threshold voltage.
  • Explain low-frequency and high-frequency C-V curves and their shifts.
  • Derive and use MOSFET linear-region, saturation-region, body-effect, and small-signal equations.
  • Connect channel charge to current and understand pinch-off without saying that current stops.

2. Ideal MOS Capacitor

Structure, work functions, flat-band condition, voltage partition, and a live visualization linking all four ideas. Section 2 Visualizer v2

2.1 Structure2.2 Work function2.3 Voltage partition

2.1 Metal-oxide-semiconductor structure

An ideal MOS capacitor has a conducting gate, a perfectly insulating oxide, and a semiconductor substrate with an ohmic back contact. The gate current is zero in the ideal electrostatic model, so every gate charge is balanced by an equal and opposite semiconductor charge.

Section 2.1 structure figure: (a) perspective view of a metal-oxide-semiconductor (MOS) capacitor and (b) cross-section showing the metal gate, SiO2 insulator, silicon substrate, applied gate voltage, oxide thickness d, depth coordinate x, and ohmic back contact.

At equilibrium, the Fermi level is constant through the metal and semiconductor. The diagram below identifies the metal work function, semiconductor work function, electron affinity, oxide barrier, bandgap, and p-type bulk potential for an ideal MOS capacitor at zero applied voltage.

Equilibrium energy-band diagram of an ideal MOS capacitor at V = 0. The common Fermi level is horizontal, while qΦm, qΦs, qχ, qχi, qΦB, Eg/2, and qψB mark the principal energy differences across the metal-oxide-semiconductor stack.
Ideal assumptions
  • No mobile charge in the oxide
  • No interface traps
  • No fixed oxide charge
  • No dc current through the oxide
  • Uniform substrate doping
Charge neutrality
\[Q_G+Q_S=0\]

For a real SiO\(_2\)-Si device, oxide and interface charge add extra terms.

2.2 Work function and flat-band voltage

The work function is the energy required to move an electron from the Fermi level to vacuum. A gate-semiconductor work-function difference creates an internal voltage even when the external terminal voltage is zero.

\[\Phi_{ms}=\Phi_m-\Phi_s,\qquad V_{FB}=\Phi_{ms}\quad\text{(ideal oxide)}\]
Work-function difference and flat-band condition. The common vacuum level defines the metal work function \(q\Phi_m\) and semiconductor work function \(q\Phi_s\). Their difference is \(\Phi_{ms}=\Phi_m-\Phi_s\). For an ideal oxide, applying \(V_{FB}=\Phi_{ms}\) cancels the initial Fermi-level offset and produces flat semiconductor bands.

At flat band, the semiconductor energy bands are spatially flat, the surface potential is zero, and the semiconductor space charge is zero. Flat band does not necessarily occur at zero applied voltage.

2.3 Voltage partition

The applied gate-to-body voltage divides between the oxide and semiconductor:

\[V_{GB}=V_{FB}+V_{ox}+\psi_s,\qquad V_{ox}=-\frac{Q_s}{C_{ox}}\]
\[C_{ox}=\frac{\varepsilon_{ox}}{t_{ox}}\]
MOS voltage partition. The applied gate-to-body voltage is divided into the built-in flat-band offset, the voltage drop across the oxide, and the semiconductor surface potential: \(V_{GB}=V_{FB}+V_{ox}+\psi_s\). Because \(V_{ox}=-Q_s/C_{ox}\), the oxide drop directly reflects the semiconductor charge, while \(\psi_s\) represents band bending.
Sign discipline. This chapter uses a p-type substrate for nMOS. Positive surface potential means the bands bend downward near the SiO\(_2\)-Si interface, promoting electron inversion.

3. Accumulation, Depletion, and Inversion

Three surface regimes viewed through charge and energy bands.

For a p-type substrate, the sign and magnitude of the gate voltage determine whether holes accumulate at the interface, a depletion region forms, or an electron inversion layer appears. The uploaded band diagrams below are used directly to illustrate these three regimes.

Accumulation

Negative gate bias: V < 0

A negative gate bias attracts majority-carrier holes to the Si-SiO2 interface. The semiconductor bands bend upward, and the hole density near the surface increases strongly.

Depletion

Moderate positive bias: V > 0

A modest positive gate repels holes from the surface, leaving behind fixed ionized acceptors. The semiconductor bands bend downward, and a depletion region develops near the interface.

Inversion

Large positive bias: V >> 0

At sufficiently large positive gate bias, electrons are attracted to the surface and form an inversion layer. The depletion width is near its maximum, and the surface behaves like n-type silicon.

How to read these band diagrams.
  • EC and EV are the conduction- and valence-band edges.
  • Ei is the intrinsic level, shown as the dashed purple curve, and EF is the Fermi level.
  • The colored circles represent the dominant carriers near the interface: holes in accumulation and electrons in inversion.
  • Upward bending corresponds to accumulation for a p-type substrate, while downward bending corresponds first to depletion and then to inversion.

Surface potential and carrier concentration

\(p_s=p_0e^{-\psi_s/V_T},\qquad n_s=n_0e^{\psi_s/V_T}\)

For a p-type substrate, the bulk Fermi potential magnitude is

\(\phi_F=V_T\ln\!\left(\frac{N_A}{n_i}\right)\)

Strong inversion is conventionally defined by \(\psi_s=2\phi_F\). At this point the surface electron concentration becomes comparable to the acceptor concentration, which is why the inversion diagram shows an electron sheet near the interface.

RegimeTypical conditionDominant semiconductor chargeBand response
Accumulation\(V_G<V_{FB}\)Mobile holes, \(Q_s>0\)Bands bend upward
Depletion\(V_{FB}<V_G<V_T\)Fixed acceptor ions, \(Q_s<0\)Bands bend downward
Strong inversion\(V_G\gtrsim V_T\)Depletion charge plus electron sheetSurface bends by about \(2\phi_F\)

6. Nonideal SiO₂-Si MOS Capacitor

Work-function difference, flat-band voltage, interface traps, fixed charge, mobile ions, and flat-band shift.

6.1 Flat-band voltage from the energy-band picture

The flat-band voltage is easiest to understand as an energy-band alignment problem. Start from the isolated metal and semiconductor, examine the voltage partition under a general gate bias, and then identify the special bias that makes the semiconductor bands flat. The three figures below show that sequence.

\[\Phi_{ms}=\Phi_M-\Phi_S\qquad V_{FB}=\Phi_{ms}-\frac{Q_{ox}}{C_{ox}}\]
Step 1. Isolated materials

With a common vacuum reference, the metal work function is \(q\Phi_M\) and the semiconductor work function is \(q\Phi_S\). For a p-type substrate, \(\Phi_S\) is larger than the electron affinity because it also includes the band-gap position and the Fermi-potential term \(\phi_F\).

Step 2. General gate bias

Away from flat band, the applied bias partitions into a flat-band offset, an oxide drop, and a semiconductor surface potential. That is why the useful voltage-partition relation is \(V_G=V_{FB}+V_{ox}+\psi_s\).

Step 3. Apply the flat-band voltage

When the device is biased so that \(V_G=V_{FB}\), the semiconductor bands are flat: \(\psi_s=0\), there is no depletion or inversion charge, and the semiconductor charge is ideally \(Q_s=0\). In an ideal MOS capacitor, this bias exactly cancels the work-function mismatch.

How to read the three figures.
  1. Isolated metal and semiconductor: determine \(\Phi_M\) and \(\Phi_S\) from the vacuum level. Their difference gives the ideal work-function term \(\Phi_{ms}\).
  2. General gate bias: after the MOS structure is formed, the applied gate voltage partitions into the flat-band offset, oxide voltage, and semiconductor surface potential: \(V_G=V_{FB}+V_{ox}+\psi_s\).
  3. Flat-band condition: set the gate bias to the value that removes semiconductor band bending. At flat band, \(\psi_s=0\) and the semiconductor charge is ideally zero, so \(V_G=V_{FB}\).
Flat-band interpretation. For an ideal oxide with no effective oxide charge, \(V_{FB}=\Phi_{ms}\). If \(\Phi_M>\Phi_S\), the required flat-band voltage is positive; if \(\Phi_M<\Phi_S\), it is negative. In measured MOS capacitors, however, the observed flat-band voltage is often shifted by oxide or interface charge.

6.2 Effective charge categories and flat-band shift

Fixed oxide charge

Usually near the interface and often positive. It translates the C-V curve along the voltage axis and shifts \(V_{FB}\).

Interface-trap charge

Energy-distributed states at the interface can exchange charge with the semiconductor, producing stretch-out, hysteresis, and frequency dependence in addition to a flat-band shift.

Mobile ionic charge

Ions can drift through the oxide under field and temperature, causing instability, bias-history dependence, and time-varying shifts in \(V_{FB}\).

Oxide-trapped charge and process-induced defects can also contribute. A useful lumped model places an effective areal charge \(Q_{ox}\) near the interface, which modifies the ideal work-function result.

\[V_{FB}=\Phi_{ms}-\frac{Q_{ox}}{C_{ox}}\]
Direction of shift. Positive oxide charge makes \(V_{FB}\) and the nMOS threshold more negative; negative oxide charge shifts them more positive.

6.3 Interface traps

Interface traps do not always behave like a simple fixed sheet. Their occupancy depends on the surface Fermi level and on measurement time scale. In C-V data, they often broaden the transition rather than only translating it, which is why nonideal C-V curves can show both shift and stretch-out.

\[D_{it}=\frac{1}{q}\frac{dQ_{it}}{dE}\quad [\mathrm{cm^{-2}eV^{-1}}]\]

7. Carrier Transport and Dielectric Breakdown

Direct tunneling, Fowler-Nordheim tunneling, emission mechanisms, and reliability.

7.1 Conduction mechanisms

MechanismDominant conditionPhysical picture
Direct tunnelingVery thin oxide, high fieldElectron wavefunction tunnels through the full oxide barrier.
Fowler-Nordheim tunnelingHigh field, triangular barrierElectrons tunnel through a field-thinned portion of the barrier.
Thermionic emissionHigh temperatureCarriers gain enough thermal energy to go over a barrier.
Poole-Frenkel emissionTraps plus electric fieldField lowers the Coulombic barrier for emission from a trap.
Schottky emissionMetal-insulator interfaceImage-force barrier lowering assists thermionic emission.
\[E_{ox}\approx\frac{V_{ox}}{t_{ox}}\]

As oxide thickness is scaled, the same voltage produces a larger electric field. Modern gate stacks therefore use high-\(k\) dielectrics to obtain large capacitance with a physically thicker film.

7.2 Breakdown

Defect generation can form a percolation path through the dielectric. Time-dependent dielectric breakdown is statistical: a device can survive for a long time and then fail after a connected defect path forms.

Reliability distinction. Breakdown is not the same as ordinary gate leakage. Leakage may be measurable while the oxide still insulates; breakdown creates a persistent conductive path and often irreversible damage.

8. MOSFET Structure and Channel Formation

n-channel structure, inversion-channel formation, and the origin of the local channel-charge equation.

An n-channel MOSFET uses two n+ source/drain regions in a p-type body. When \(V_{GS}>V_T\), the gate attracts electrons to the oxide–silicon interface and forms a conducting inversion channel. The channel charge decreases from source to drain as the local channel potential \(V(x)\) rises.

n-channel MOSFET structure and inversion-channel model. The figure derives \(Q_i(x)=-C_{ox}[V_{GS}-V_T-V(x)]\), identifies the source- and drain-end channel charge, and explains why the inversion charge approaches zero at pinch-off.
Key physical connection. The gate and the local inversion layer behave approximately as a parallel-plate capacitor. Increasing \(V(x)\) toward the drain reduces the local oxide voltage and therefore reduces the magnitude of the negative inversion charge.

9. MOSFET I-V Characteristics

Gradual-channel derivation, linear region, saturation, and channel-length modulation.

9.1 Current from inversion charge

Under the gradual-channel approximation, the lateral field is much smaller than the vertical gate field. The drift current is approximately constant along the channel:

\[I_D=-W\mu_n Q_i(x)\frac{dV}{dx}\]
Integrate from source to drain.
\[I_D=\mu_n C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}\left[(V_{GS}-V_T)V_{DS}-\frac{V_{DS}^2}{2}\right]\]

9.2 Region equations

\[\boxed{I_D=\mu_n C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}\left[V_{OV}V_{DS}-\frac{V_{DS}^2}{2}\right](1+\lambda V_{DS})}\quad 0\le V_{DS}<V_{OV}\]
\[\boxed{I_D=\frac{1}{2}\mu_nC_{ox}\frac{W}{L}V_{OV}^2(1+\lambda V_{DS})}\quad V_{DS}\ge V_{OV}\]

Here \(V_{OV}=V_{GS}-V_T\). Channel-length modulation \(\lambda\) gives the saturation curve a finite slope because the effective channel length shortens as the drain depletion region expands.

10. Body Effect, Capacitances, and Charge

Threshold modulation, intrinsic capacitances, and switching implications.

10.1 Body effect

A positive source-to-body voltage reverse-biases the source-body junction, increasing the depletion charge required for inversion. The threshold voltage rises:

\[V_T(V_{SB})=V_{T0}+\gamma\left(\sqrt{2\phi_F+V_{SB}}-\sqrt{2\phi_F}\right)\]

10.2 Intrinsic capacitances

The gate charge is distributed among source, drain, body, and overlap regions. In the long-channel approximation:

RegionApproximate intrinsic capacitance picture
CutoffGate couples mainly to body through oxide and depletion capacitances.
LinearChannel spans source to drain; roughly \(C_{gs}\approx C_{gd}\approx \tfrac12 C_{ox}WL\) before overlap corrections.
SaturationChannel is pinched off at drain; \(C_{gd}\) becomes small and \(C_{gs}\approx \tfrac23 C_{ox}WL\) in the simple charge-partition model.
Switching implication. A transistor can have excellent dc current but still switch slowly if the driver must repeatedly charge a large gate capacitance. Dynamic energy is roughly \(E\approx C_GV^2\) per full charge-discharge cycle.

11. Small-Signal MOSFET Model

Transconductance, output resistance, body transconductance, and gain.

11.1 Linearization around a bias point

In saturation, a small change in gate voltage produces a drain-current change described by transconductance:

\[g_m=\frac{\partial I_D}{\partial V_{GS}}=\mu_nC_{ox}\frac{W}{L}V_{OV}=\frac{2I_D}{V_{OV}}\]
\[g_{ds}=\frac{\partial I_D}{\partial V_{DS}}\approx\lambda I_D,\qquad r_o=\frac{1}{g_{ds}}\]

Body-effect transconductance is commonly written \(g_{mb}=\eta g_m\), where \(\eta\) depends on \(\gamma\), \(\phi_F\), and body bias.

Intrinsic voltage gain
\[A_{v0}\approx g_mr_o\]

Higher \(g_m\) and larger \(r_o\) increase gain.

Efficiency metric
\[\frac{g_m}{I_D}=\frac{2}{V_{OV}}\]

Lower overdrive gives larger transconductance efficiency in strong inversion, but less speed and current density.

Model range. The square-law equations are pedagogically valuable but not quantitatively exact for short-channel modern transistors. Velocity saturation, mobility degradation, DIBL, and quantum confinement alter the behavior.

12. Numerical Design Workflow

A structured route from process parameters to operating point and performance.

  1. Define process parameters: \(t_{ox}\), dielectric constant, \(N_A\), work-function difference, oxide charge, and mobility.
  2. Compute MOS electrostatics: \(C_{ox}\), \(\phi_F\), \(\gamma\), \(V_{FB}\), and \(V_T\).
  3. Apply terminal voltages: use body effect to update threshold, then determine cutoff, linear, or saturation region.
  4. Calculate current: use the appropriate I-V expression and verify the assumed region.
  5. Extract small-signal terms: compute \(g_m\), \(r_o\), and capacitances around the operating point.
  6. Check physical limits: oxide field, power, current density, and whether long-channel assumptions remain reasonable.
Assume → solve → verify

Always state the region assumption before using a region equation. After solving, check that \(V_{DS}<V_{OV}\) for linear operation or \(V_{DS}\ge V_{OV}\) for saturation.
